name: Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation
description: Gives the ideal change in velocity (delta-v) a rocket can achieve as the exhaust velocity times the natural log of the initial-to-final mass ratio. It shows why carrying more propellant yields diminishing returns in speed.
notes: Ignores gravity and drag losses, so real missions need more propellant than it implies. Initial mass must exceed final mass, and both masses must use the same units.

name: Ideal Rocket Nozzle Exhaust Velocity
description: Computes the ideal exhaust velocity of gas leaving a rocket nozzle from thermodynamic conditions. It follows the isentropic expansion relation using the specific heat ratio, chamber temperature, molar mass, and the exit-to-chamber pressure ratio, giving the theoretical maximum jet speed.
notes: Assumes ideal, isentropic, one-dimensional flow of a perfect gas; real velocities are somewhat lower. R here is the universal gas constant, divided internally by molar mass M; pressures must be absolute.

name: Effective Exhaust Velocity from Specific Impulse
description: Converts specific impulse into effective exhaust velocity. It equals the specific impulse times standard gravity, since specific impulse expressed in seconds is the exhaust velocity divided by standard gravity.
notes: This uses Isp defined in seconds; multiplying by g0 (9.80665 m/s^2) recovers the velocity. g0 is a fixed reference constant, not the local gravity at the vehicle.

name: Rocket Thrust Equation
description: Computes total rocket thrust as the sum of momentum and pressure terms. It equals the mass flow rate times exhaust velocity plus the exit-minus-ambient pressure difference times the nozzle exit area, so ambient pressure affects thrust.
notes: Thrust is highest in vacuum where ambient pressure is zero; at sea level the pressure term can subtract from thrust. Use absolute pressures for both exit and ambient values.

name: Thrust-to-Weight Ratio
description: Gives the dimensionless thrust-to-weight ratio of a vehicle. It equals the thrust divided by the vehicle mass times standard gravity, indicating whether the vehicle can lift off (ratio above one) or accelerate upward.
notes: The result is dimensionless; a value above 1 means thrust exceeds weight. Weight is computed with standard gravity g0, so the ratio is referenced to Earth sea-level weight.

name: Specific Impulse from Thrust
description: Computes specific impulse in seconds from measured thrust and propellant flow. It equals the thrust divided by the mass flow rate times standard gravity, expressing how efficiently propellant mass is turned into impulse.
notes: Result is in seconds because it is referenced to standard gravity g0; higher values mean more impulse per unit propellant mass. Mass flow rate must be the total propellant flow.

name: Rocket Mass Ratio from Delta-v
description: Gives the required initial-to-final mass ratio for a rocket to achieve a target delta-v. It equals the exponential of delta-v divided by the effective exhaust velocity, from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
notes: Result is the ratio of wet mass to dry mass and is always greater than one. Because it grows exponentially, high delta-v missions demand disproportionately large propellant fractions.

name: Propellant Mass Fraction
description: Gives the fraction of total rocket mass that must be propellant to achieve a given delta-v. It equals one minus the exponential of minus delta-v divided by the effective exhaust velocity, derived from the rocket equation.
notes: Result is a fraction between 0 and 1 of the initial mass. High delta-v pushes this fraction toward 1, leaving little mass for structure and payload.

name: Characteristic Velocity (c-star)
description: Gives the characteristic velocity c-star, a measure of combustion efficiency independent of the nozzle. It equals the chamber pressure times the throat area divided by the mass flow rate, reflecting how effectively the propellant releases energy in the chamber.
notes: c-star depends on chamber and propellant properties, not on nozzle expansion; it isolates combustion performance from thrust generation. Use absolute chamber pressure and the geometric throat area.

name: Nozzle Thrust Coefficient
description: Gives the nozzle thrust coefficient, which measures how much the nozzle amplifies chamber pressure into thrust. It equals the thrust divided by the chamber pressure times the throat area, isolating nozzle expansion performance.
notes: The coefficient is dimensionless and captures nozzle performance separately from combustion (c-star). Use absolute chamber pressure and the geometric throat area.

name: Isentropic Nozzle Area Ratio
description: Gives the ratio of nozzle exit area to throat area needed to reach a target exit Mach number in isentropic flow. It follows the area-Mach relation using the exit Mach number and specific heat ratio, growing rapidly for supersonic exits.
notes: Assumes isentropic, one-dimensional flow of a perfect gas. The relation is double-valued in Mach number; this form gives the supersonic-branch area ratio for M greater than one.

name: Ballistic Coefficient
description: Gives the ballistic coefficient of a body, a measure of its ability to overcome air resistance. It equals the mass divided by the drag coefficient times the reference area, so heavy, slender, low-drag bodies decelerate less in the atmosphere.
notes: A higher value means the body retains speed better against drag. The result depends on the chosen reference area, which must match the one used to define the drag coefficient.

name: Choked Nozzle Critical Pressure Ratio
description: Gives the critical exit-to-chamber pressure ratio at which a converging nozzle chokes and the throat reaches Mach one. It equals two over gamma plus one, raised to gamma over gamma minus one, depending only on the specific heat ratio.
notes: Below this pressure ratio the flow is choked and mass flow no longer increases with further downstream pressure drop. It depends solely on gamma, not on absolute pressures.

name: Allen-Eggers Peak Deceleration
description: Estimates the peak deceleration experienced by a ballistic entry vehicle using the Allen-Eggers solution. It equals the entry velocity squared times the atmospheric scale factor times the sine of the flight path angle divided by twice Euler's number, giving the maximum g-load during reentry.
notes: The result is independent of vehicle mass and ballistic coefficient, a key Allen-Eggers finding; it assumes a steep, straight-line entry through an exponential atmosphere. The e in the denominator is Euler's number.

name: Sutton-Graves Stagnation Heat Flux
description: Estimates the convective stagnation-point heat flux on a reentry vehicle using the Sutton-Graves correlation. It equals an empirical constant times the square root of free-stream density over nose radius times the velocity cubed, so heating scales with the cube of speed.
notes: An empirical engineering correlation; the constant is calibrated for air and the result is in W/cm^2. A larger nose radius lowers heating, which is why blunt bodies are used for reentry.

name: Nozzle Exit Static Temperature
description: Computes the static temperature of exhaust gas at the nozzle exit after isentropic expansion. It equals the chamber temperature times the exit-to-chamber pressure ratio raised to gamma minus one over gamma, showing how the gas cools as it expands.
notes: Assumes isentropic flow of a perfect gas; temperatures must be absolute and pressures absolute. The exit gas is always cooler than the chamber because expansion converts thermal energy to kinetic energy.

name: Rocket Propulsive Efficiency
description: Gives the propulsive efficiency of a rocket, the fraction of jet kinetic energy converted into useful vehicle thrust power. It equals twice the vehicle-to-exhaust speed ratio divided by one plus that ratio squared, peaking when vehicle speed equals exhaust velocity.
notes: The result is a dimensionless efficiency between 0 and 1, maximized (equal to 1) when vehicle speed matches exhaust velocity. Both speeds should be in the same reference frame and units.

name: Combustion Chamber Characteristic Length
description: Gives the characteristic length L-star of a rocket combustion chamber, a measure of residence time for the propellant. It equals the chamber volume divided by the throat area, used to size chambers for complete combustion.
notes: L-star sets the gas residence time before the throat; too small a value risks incomplete combustion. It is a design parameter specific to the propellant combination.

name: Net Vehicle Acceleration
description: Computes the net upward acceleration of a launch vehicle against gravity. It equals the thrust divided by the vehicle mass minus the gravitational acceleration, giving the actual acceleration available for climb after gravity is overcome.
notes: This is a vertical-flight estimate that subtracts full gravity; it ignores aerodynamic drag and thrust vector angle. A positive result requires thrust to exceed instantaneous weight.

name: Total Impulse from Specific Impulse
description: Computes a rocket's total impulse, the time-integrated thrust, as the product of specific impulse, standard gravity, and expelled propellant mass. It measures the overall momentum change the engine delivers over the whole burn.
notes: Specific impulse must be expressed in seconds (the g0 form); using effective exhaust velocity instead would drop the g0 factor. Result is in newton-seconds and assumes complete consumption of the propellant mass.

name: Gravity Loss (Vertical Ascent)
description: Estimates the velocity lost to gravity during a powered ascent as gravity times the sine of the flight path angle times the burn time. It quantifies how much delta-v is spent fighting gravity rather than accelerating the vehicle.
notes: Assumes constant gravity and a constant flight path angle over the burn; gamma is in radians, with sin(gamma)=1 for a purely vertical climb. Real ascents integrate a varying angle.

name: Vis-Viva Equation
description: Gives the orbital speed at a point in a two-body orbit from the gravitational parameter, the current radial distance, and the semi-major axis. It links speed, position, and orbit size for any conic orbit.
notes: All lengths in meters and mu in m^3/s^2 for a result in m/s. For a circle r equals a; for hyperbolic orbits a is negative. It ignores perturbations and other bodies.

name: Standard Gravitational Parameter
description: Computes the standard gravitational parameter mu as the gravitational constant times the mass of the central body. This product appears throughout orbital mechanics and is known far more precisely than G or M individually.
notes: Result is in m^3/s^2 when G and M use SI units. In practice mu is measured directly from spacecraft tracking rather than from G times M, which carries G's large uncertainty.

name: Specific Orbital Energy
description: Gives the specific orbital energy (total energy per unit mass) of a two-body orbit as minus mu divided by twice the semi-major axis. It stays constant along the orbit and sets the orbit's size.
notes: Negative for bound (elliptical) orbits, zero for parabolic, positive for hyperbolic where a is negative. Result is energy per unit mass (J/kg), independent of the orbiting body's mass.

name: Specific Angular Momentum (Elliptical Orbit)
description: Computes the specific angular momentum of an elliptical orbit from the gravitational parameter, semi-major axis, and eccentricity. This conserved quantity fixes the orbit's shape and the swept-area rate.
notes: Eccentricity is dimensionless and must satisfy 0<=ecc<1 for a bound orbit, or the term under the root turns negative. Result is in m^2/s.

name: Semi-Latus Rectum
description: Computes the semi-latus rectum of a conic orbit as the semi-major axis times (1 minus eccentricity squared). It is the orbit radius at true anomaly of 90 degrees and serves as the scale parameter in the orbit equation.
notes: For a circle it equals a; for higher eccentricity it shrinks. For a parabola use the direct definition since a is infinite. Length units follow a.

name: Apoapsis Radius
description: Gives the apoapsis radius, the greatest distance from the focus in an elliptical orbit, as the semi-major axis times (1 plus eccentricity). This is the farthest point of the orbit from the central body's center.
notes: This is measured from the center of the central body, not its surface; subtract the body radius for altitude. Requires 0<=ecc<1. Length units follow a.

name: Periapsis Radius
description: Gives the periapsis radius, the closest distance to the focus in an elliptical orbit, as the semi-major axis times (1 minus eccentricity). This is the nearest point of the orbit to the central body's center.
notes: Measured from the central body's center, not its surface; subtract the body radius for altitude and check it clears the surface. Requires 0<=ecc<1.

name: Eccentricity from Apsides
description: Computes the orbital eccentricity from the apoapsis and periapsis radii as their difference divided by their sum. It gives a dimensionless measure of how elongated the orbit is from these two extreme radii.
notes: Both radii must be measured from the same focus (the central body's center) in the same units; the units cancel. Result is 0 for a circle and approaches 1 for a very elongated ellipse.

name: Hohmann Transfer Total Delta-v
description: Computes the total delta-v for a two-burn Hohmann transfer between two coplanar circular orbits, summing the speed change at departure and at arrival. It gives the minimum impulsive cost for such a transfer.
notes: Assumes coplanar circular start and end orbits and instantaneous burns; r1 and r2 are radii from the center. It is not optimal when the radius ratio exceeds about 11.94, where a bi-elliptic transfer can be cheaper.

name: Hohmann Transfer Time
description: Gives the flight time of a Hohmann transfer as half the period of the transfer ellipse, from the two circular orbit radii and the gravitational parameter. It is the coast time between the departure and arrival burns.
notes: Equals half the transfer-ellipse orbital period, since the transfer covers 180 degrees. Lengths in meters and mu in m^3/s^2 give seconds. Assumes coplanar circular endpoints.

name: Geostationary Orbit Radius
description: Computes the orbital radius at which the period equals a given sidereal rotation period, from Kepler's third law using the gravitational parameter. At this radius a satellite stays fixed over a point on the equator.
notes: Result is radius from the body's center, not altitude; subtract the equatorial radius for height above the surface. Use the sidereal day (about 86164 s for Earth), not the 86400 s solar day.

name: Hyperbolic Excess Velocity
description: Computes the hyperbolic excess velocity, the speed remaining infinitely far from the body, from the burnout velocity, gravitational parameter, and burnout radius. It is the leftover speed after fully escaping the gravity well.
notes: Requires burnout speed above escape speed, so the term under the root stays positive; otherwise the orbit is bound and there is no real excess velocity. Result is in m/s.

name: Characteristic Energy (C3)
description: Computes the characteristic energy C3, twice the specific orbital energy, as minus mu divided by the semi-major axis. It equals the square of the hyperbolic excess velocity and measures the energy of an escape trajectory.
notes: For an escape trajectory a is negative, making C3 positive; C3 equals v-infinity squared. Result is in m^2/s^2. Zero C3 corresponds to a parabolic (marginal escape) orbit.

name: Laplace Sphere of Influence
description: Estimates the radius of a planet's sphere of influence by Laplace's formula, as the orbital radius times the mass ratio of planet to Sun raised to the two-fifths power. Inside it the planet's gravity dominates over the Sun's.
notes: The mass ratio is planet mass over central (Sun) mass, and the exponent is 2/5. It marks the boundary used in patched-conic approximations, not a sharp physical edge.

name: Hill Sphere Radius
description: Estimates the Hill sphere radius, the region where a body's gravity dominates for retaining satellites, from the periapsis distance and the cube root of the mass ratio to the primary. It bounds stable orbits around the smaller body.
notes: Uses periapsis distance a(1-ecc), so it gives the tightest (smallest) Hill radius over the orbit. The mass ratio is secondary over three times the primary. Retrograde satellites can remain stable somewhat beyond this radius.

name: Mean Motion
description: Computes the mean motion, the average angular rate of an orbiting body, as the square root of mu divided by the semi-major axis cubed. It is the mean anomaly's rate of change and equals two pi over the orbital period.
notes: Result is in radians per second with SI inputs. It describes the uniform average rate, not the instantaneous angular speed, which varies over an eccentric orbit.

name: Kepler's Equation (Mean Anomaly)
description: Computes the mean anomaly from the eccentric anomaly and eccentricity via Kepler's equation, mean anomaly equals eccentric anomaly minus eccentricity times its sine. It relates uniform time progression to position on the ellipse.
notes: This is the direct (forward) form; finding eccentric anomaly from mean anomaly requires iteration. Angles are in radians and eccentricity is dimensionless with 0<=ecc<1.

name: True Anomaly from Eccentric Anomaly
description: Converts the eccentric anomaly to the true anomaly using the eccentricity, giving the actual angular position of the body from periapsis as seen from the focus. It maps the auxiliary-circle angle to the real orbital angle.
notes: The half-angle tangent form avoids quadrant ambiguity when used with atan2; a plain atan may need a quadrant correction. Angles in radians, 0<=ecc<1.

name: Flight Path Angle
description: Computes the flight path angle from eccentricity and true anomaly, the angle between the velocity vector and the local horizontal (perpendicular to the radius). It shows how steeply the body climbs or descends along its orbit.
notes: It is zero at periapsis and apoapsis, positive while moving outward and negative inward. Angles in radians; the result is bounded even for high eccentricity.

name: Orbit Radius from True Anomaly
description: Gives the orbital radius at a given true anomaly from the semi-major axis, eccentricity, and true anomaly, via the conic orbit equation. It returns the distance from the focus to the body at that angular position.
notes: Radius is measured from the focus (central body's center). At nu=0 it gives periapsis and at nu=pi apoapsis. Angle in radians, 0<=ecc<1.

name: Speed at Periapsis
description: Computes the orbital speed at periapsis, the fastest point of an elliptical orbit, from the gravitational parameter, semi-major axis, and eccentricity. It is the maximum speed the body reaches over one revolution.
notes: Valid for 0<=ecc<1; speed rises sharply as eccentricity approaches 1. This is the vis-viva speed evaluated at periapsis radius. Result in m/s with SI inputs.

name: Speed at Apoapsis
description: Computes the orbital speed at apoapsis, the slowest point of an elliptical orbit, from the gravitational parameter, semi-major axis, and eccentricity. It is the minimum speed the body reaches over one revolution.
notes: Valid for 0<=ecc<1; the apoapsis speed drops toward zero as eccentricity approaches 1. This is the vis-viva speed at apoapsis radius. Result in m/s.

name: Circular Velocity at Altitude
description: Computes the speed needed to maintain a circular orbit at a given altitude, from the gravitational parameter and the orbital radius (body radius plus altitude). It is the constant speed that balances gravity for a circular path.
notes: The orbital radius is the body's radius plus altitude, both from the center. Assumes a circular orbit and no atmospheric drag or perturbations. Result in m/s.

name: Orbital Period at Altitude
description: Computes the orbital period of a circular orbit at a given altitude from the orbital radius (body radius plus altitude) and the gravitational parameter, following Kepler's third law. It is the time for one full revolution.
notes: Uses radius from the center (body radius plus altitude), not altitude alone. Assumes a circular orbit; for an ellipse use the semi-major axis. Result in seconds.

name: Escape Velocity at Altitude
description: Computes the escape velocity at a given altitude from the gravitational parameter and orbital radius (body radius plus altitude). It is the minimum speed needed to escape the body's gravity from that point, ignoring drag.
notes: Equals the square root of two times the local circular speed. Radius is body radius plus altitude from the center. Direction-independent and ignores atmospheric drag and other bodies.

name: Roche Limit (Fluid Body)
description: Computes the Roche limit for a fluid satellite, the distance within which tidal forces would tear it apart, from the primary's radius and the cube root of the density ratio (primary to satellite). It uses the 2.44 fluid-body coefficient.
notes: The 2.44 coefficient applies to a fluid, deformable satellite; rigid bodies held by material strength use a smaller factor near 1.26. Distance is measured from the primary's center.

name: Synchronous Orbit Altitude
description: Computes the altitude of a synchronous orbit above the surface, from the gravitational parameter, the body's rotation period, and its radius. It is the synchronous orbital radius from Kepler's third law minus the body radius.
notes: Use the sidereal rotation period. The result is altitude above the surface, since the body radius is already subtracted from the synchronous radius. SI inputs give meters.

name: Tisserand Parameter
description: Computes the Tisserand parameter with respect to a perturbing planet from that planet's semi-major axis, the object's semi-major axis, eccentricity, and inclination. It stays nearly constant through close encounters and helps classify small-body orbits.
notes: The semi-major axes must share the same unit (they appear only as a ratio); inclination is in radians. It is conserved only approximately in the circular restricted three-body problem.

name: J2 Nodal Precession Rate
description: Computes the rate of nodal precession (regression of the ascending node) caused by a body's J2 oblateness, from the mean motion, J2, the ratio of body radius to semi-latus rectum, and the inclination. It drives sun-synchronous orbit design.
notes: Inclination is in radians; the rate is negative (westward) for prograde orbits and vanishes at 90 degrees. Result in rad/s. Captures only the dominant J2 term, not higher harmonics.

name: J2 Apsidal Precession Rate
description: Computes the rate of apsidal precession (rotation of the line of apsides) caused by J2 oblateness, from the mean motion, J2, the ratio of body radius to semi-latus rectum, and the inclination. It governs how the periapsis argument drifts.
notes: Inclination is in radians; the rate vanishes at the critical inclination of about 63.4 degrees, where 4-5sin^2(i)=0, a property exploited by Molniya orbits. Result in rad/s.

name: Specific Kinetic Energy (Circular Orbit)
description: Gives the specific kinetic energy (kinetic energy per unit mass) of a circular orbit as mu divided by twice the orbit radius. It equals half the local circular speed squared and, for a circular orbit, the magnitude of the total specific energy.
notes: Valid for circular orbits only, where speed equals the circular velocity. Result is J/kg, independent of the orbiting mass. Radius is from the central body's center.

name: Specific Angular Momentum (Circular Orbit)
description: Computes the specific angular momentum of a circular orbit as the square root of the gravitational parameter times the orbit radius. For a circle this equals the orbit radius times the circular speed.
notes: Valid for circular orbits; for an ellipse use the semi-major axis and eccentricity form instead. Result in m^2/s, independent of the orbiting body's mass.

name: Orbital Resonance Period Ratio
description: Computes the ratio of orbital periods for two bodies from the ratio of their semi-major axes raised to the three-halves power, following Kepler's third law. It reveals whether two orbits are near a simple integer resonance.
notes: The two semi-major axes must use the same unit; only their ratio matters. It assumes both orbits circle the same central body. A near-integer result indicates a mean-motion resonance.

name: Two-Body Orbital Period (Reduced Mass)
description: Computes the orbital period of a two-body system from the semi-major axis of the relative orbit and the sum of the two masses, using the gravitational constant. Unlike the restricted case, it accounts for both bodies' masses.
notes: The semi-major axis is that of the relative orbit (separation between the bodies). Using the mass sum makes it exact for comparable masses. SI inputs give seconds.

name: L1 Lagrange Point Distance (Approx)
description: Estimates the distance from the smaller body to the L1 Lagrange point as the primary separation times the cube root of the secondary-to-three-times-primary mass ratio. It approximates where the two gravities and orbital motion balance.
notes: This first-order approximation holds when the secondary is much lighter than the primary; L1 and L2 sit at nearly this distance on opposite sides. Distance is measured from the secondary body.

name: Semi-Major Axis from Apsides
description: Computes the semi-major axis of an elliptical orbit as the average of the apoapsis and periapsis radii. The major axis spans both apsides, so half their sum gives the semi-major axis.
notes: Both radii must be measured from the same focus (the central body's center) in the same units. This is the geometric average of the two apsidal radii, not of their altitudes.

name: Simple Plane-Change Delta-v
description: Computes the delta-v required for a simple plane-change maneuver that rotates the velocity vector by an inclination change di while holding orbital speed v constant, as Δv = 2v·sin(Δi/2).
notes: di is entered in degrees and converted internally to radians before the sine. Plane changes are cheapest where orbital speed v is lowest, such as at apoapsis of an elliptical orbit.

name: Sun-Synchronous Orbit Inclination
description: Gives the inclination at which Earth's oblateness turns a circular orbit's plane once a year, keeping the same local solar time — used by Earth-observation satellites.
notes: At 700 km it is about 98.2°.

name: Ground Track Shift per Orbit
description: Gives how far west the ground track moves each orbit because Earth rotates underneath.
notes: The ISS track shifts about 23° per orbit.

name: Slant Range to a Satellite at the Horizon
description: Gives the longest line-of-sight distance to a satellite, when it is just on the horizon.
notes: Starlink-type satellites at 550 km can be up to about 2700 km away.

name: Gravity Assist Maximum Velocity Change
description: Gives the change in a spacecraft's velocity (in the planet's frame direction) from a flyby: 2v∞ sin(δ/2).
notes: Closer passes of heavier planets bend the path more.

name: Multi-Stage Rocket Total Delta-v
description: Adds the Tsiolkovsky delta-v of each rocket stage to get the total the vehicle can achieve.
notes: Low Earth orbit needs about 9.4 km/s including losses.

name: Orbital Drag Deceleration
description: Gives the deceleration of a satellite from the thin upper atmosphere, which slowly lowers its orbit.
notes: Upper-air density varies tenfold with solar activity.

name: Bi-Elliptic Transfer Total Delta-v
expression: sqrt(mu / r1) * (sqrt(2 * rb / (r1 + rb)) - 1) + sqrt(mu / rb) * (sqrt(2 * r2 / (rb + r2)) - sqrt(2 * r1 / (r1 + rb))) + sqrt(mu / r2) * (sqrt(2 * rb / (rb + r2)) - 1)
description: Gives the total delta-v of a three-burn bi-elliptic transfer between circular orbits.
notes: Beats a Hohmann transfer only when r₂/r₁ exceeds about 11.94 — at the cost of much more time.
